title: Credit Score Prediction
description: Developed and benchmarked multiclass credit-score classifiers on 25,000 initial customer-month records, comparing 8 model/feature-set combinations. The selected XGBoost model reached 0.6898 macro F1 and 70.79% accuracy on a 4,577-row group-disjoint evaluation set.
problemStatement: Predict customer credit-score categories (Good, Poor, and Standard) from financial behavior and credit history. Compare four machine learning algorithms and two feature-set strategies using customer-disjoint splitting and macro-averaged metrics.
businessContext: Credit scoring is a multiclass risk categorization task. This academic study explores how supervised learning may help analysts organize credit-risk patterns. It is not a validated lending decision system or a substitute for appropriate financial and fairness reviews.
dataset: Credit-score customer-month dataset (data_C.csv): 25,000 original observations and 29 columns including customer profile, credit facilities, loan details, repayment behavior, balances, and the Credit_Score target. After cleaning and filtering, the notebook reports 22,412 modeling records. Personal identifiers (Name, SSN, ID) are not model predictors.
datasetSize: 25,000 original records (29 columns) · 22,412 after cleaning · 17,835 train / 4,577 test · 3 classes
preprocessing: Audited missing values, inconsistent numeric/text formatting, duplicates and financial-value anomalies across 29 original columns.
Repaired inconsistent age and credit-related values, applied customer-based data consistency checks, and retained 22,412 records after documented cleaning.
Used StratifiedGroupKFold with Customer_ID as the group variable: 7,212 train customers and 1,830 test customers with zero overlapping customers.
Constructed sklearn Pipelines and ColumnTransformers: numerical median imputation, categorical most-frequent imputation and one-hot encoding; RobustScaler for the linear-model branch.
Excluded names, social security numbers and customer identifiers from the final classification features.
featureEngineering: Experiment A — Original + Feature Engineering (32 features): constructed EMI-, investment-, balance- and debt-to-salary ratios; credit-history missingness; nine loan-type flags; and spending/payment categories.
Experiment B — Original + Loan Flags (31 features): kept 17 numerical, 5 categorical and 9 binary loan-type features; this was the best-performing feature configuration.
Encoded loan categories such as mortgage, student, payday, auto, personal and debt-consolidation loans into model-ready binary flags.
methodology: Trained and tuned four algorithms — Logistic Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost and LightGBM — on both feature-set strategies (8 total trained/evaluated combinations).
For the engineered-feature comparison, used RandomizedSearchCV with 20 candidates and 5 stratified group-aware CV folds per algorithm, optimizing macro F1.
For the original-plus-loan-flags comparison, used RandomizedSearchCV with 10 candidates and 3 group-aware CV folds per algorithm, optimizing macro F1.
Used customer-disjoint train/test partitions (17,835 / 4,577 rows); tested all models with accuracy, balanced accuracy, macro precision/recall/F1 and multiclass one-vs-rest ROC-AUC.

Selected the final saved XGBoost configuration based on the notebook-reported test macro-F1 across the two feature sets; the associated final estimate should therefore be treated as exploratory rather than an independently confirmed holdout result.
results: Best recorded configuration: XGBoost with Original + Loan Flags (31 predictors); test macro F1 = 0.6898, accuracy = 70.79%, balanced accuracy = 0.7040, macro OvR ROC-AUC = 0.8591.
XGBoost using Original + Feature Engineering achieved macro F1 = 0.6860 and accuracy = 70.44%; both feature configurations outperformed Logistic Regression on macro F1.
Evaluated all 8 algorithm/feature-set combinations on the 4,577-row test partition; highest recorded macro F1 = 0.6898.
Verified zero Customer_ID overlap between train and test (7,212 vs. 1,830 customers); saved the selected pipeline and label encoder to a Joblib model artifact.
Best XGBoost confusion-matrix diagonal: 566 Good, 896 Poor, and 1,778 Standard predictions correctly classified.
insights: Using original numerical/categorical credit variables plus explicit loan-type flags slightly outperformed the more extensively engineered ratio-feature strategy on macro F1.
The dominant Standard class (13,282 of the original 25,000 records) makes macro-averaged metrics more informative than overall accuracy alone.
Group-based splitting is important because monthly observations may refer to the same customer; this split avoids customer overlap across train and test.
A comparison of class-level confusion matrices provides more context than accuracy alone, particularly for the Good and Poor categories.
businessImpact: Potential decision support for exploratory customer credit-risk segmentation and analyst-led case prioritization. Any regulated or production credit decision would require independent validation, calibration, explainability, bias/fairness checks, legal review and monitoring.
challenges: Correcting malformed numerical values and anomalous financial fields while preserving plausible credit-risk variation.
Handling repeated customer-month observations without customer overlap in evaluation.
Comparing linear and tree-based models under mixed numerical/categorical feature types and a nonuniform class distribution.
limitations: Reported metrics are sourced from the supplied notebook and have not been independently reproduced in this documentation.
The final algorithm/feature-set was chosen using test-set macro F1; a new untouched holdout or outer group-aware validation is needed for unbiased final model selection and evaluation.
Dataset cleaning occurred before the train/test split, so some preprocessing steps warrant an additional leakage audit and migration into a train-fitted pipeline.
The source dataset contains personally identifying fields and is intentionally not redistributed in the public GitHub package.
An end-to-end deployment of this specific credit-score artifact has not been confirmed from the four files supplied here.
futureImprovements: Introduce an independent final group holdout (or nested grouped cross-validation), keeping model selection away from final test data.
Place all learned data-cleaning statistics within train-fitted pipeline stages for leakage-safe reproducibility.
Add calibrated class probabilities, group-wise error analysis, model explainability, and fairness checks before any production-oriented use.
Document separate Streamlit / MLflow / AWS deployment evidence once the implementation files are provided.

Completed a monolithic Streamlit application and a decoupled Streamlit + FastAPI architecture.
insights: All 5,000 placement labels agree with a deterministic four-threshold rule (CGPA ≥ 7, technical skill ≥ 60, soft skill ≥ 55, backlogs ≤ 2).
Tree-based classifiers identify threshold splits well; this dataset structure helps explain the perfect held-out test accuracy for the selected placement model.
The regression track was evaluated separately as a continuous-outcome task, using MAE, RMSE and R² rather than classification accuracy.
Building monolithic and decoupled applications showed two ways of connecting trained models to user-facing interfaces.
businessImpact: Demonstrates an integrated student-outcome analytics prototype: from feature analysis and ML model selection to a user-facing application and reusable prediction API.
